planting.note: Set divided crowns or rooted offsets in constantly moist, rich soil in partial shade to shade once nights stay reliably above 55°F; vegetable fern colonizes wet ditches and stream margins throughout the tropics and is killed back hard by even a light frost.

directions: Plant divided crowns in constantly moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade; vegetable fern is a fast-spreading tropical fern of Southeast Asia and the Pacific whose tightly coiled young fiddleheads and tender upper fronds are harvested every few days as a mild, slightly mucilaginous green, stir-fried, added to soups, or blanched for salads. It thrives in soggy, even seasonally flooded ground along ditches, pond edges, and rice-paddy margins, making it a useful crop for the wet, shaded corners of a warm-climate garden where few other vegetables perform. Keep the crown constantly wet and cut fronds regularly to encourage a steady flush of new, tender growth; plants die back completely at the first frost and must be grown as an annual or protected in pots outside zone 9b.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops & Plant Products
University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources (CTAHR)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in ordinary, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; jumpseed tolerates dry shade under mature trees better than most woodland perennials once established and self-sows modestly where happy.

directions: Plant in ordinary, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, including the dry shade under established trees where it tolerates competition better than most woodland perennials once its roots are established. Virginia jumpseed is a tough eastern North American native prized less for its wiry spikes of small greenish-white flowers than for its explosive seed dispersal — ripe seeds are launched several feet when the wand-like flower stalks are brushed, a trait that gives the plant its common name and makes it a fun teaching plant for children's gardens. The variegated cultivar sold as 'Painter's Palette', with a dark V-shaped chevron and creamy speckling splashed across each leaf, is grown chiefly as a striking dry-shade foliage plant and reseeds true enough to keep a colorful patch going for years. Cut plants back hard in late winter to clear the previous year's dried stems before new growth emerges.

planting.note: Plant root cuttings or young container trees in spring in average to rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; root suckers freely once established, which is the easiest way to start new plants and also how established colonies expand and are thinned for shoot harvest.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Japanese angelica tree is a large, sparsely branched, spiny-stemmed understory tree grown throughout Japan and Korea for its highly prized spring shoots — known as dureup or taranome — which are snapped off while still tightly furled, blanched or lightly battered and fried as tempura, and valued for a distinctive bittersweet, slightly resinous flavor. Established plants sucker readily from the roots to form a spreading colony, and shoot harvest is timed to remove the terminal buds from two- and three-year-old suckers each spring, which also keeps the colony to a manageable size. Left unharvested it becomes a bold architectural small tree with huge, twice-compound leaves and large plumes of white flowers in late summer followed by black berries relished by birds; variegated ornamental selections are grown for foliage alone. Give it room to sucker and site it away from foot traffic, since both stems and leaf stalks carry sharp prickles.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Direct-sow shallowly after the soil has warmed, in moist, fertile soil in partial shade; ebolo germinates and grows quickly in warm weather, self-sows readily, and can also be started from stem cuttings rooted in water.

directions: Sow or transplant into moist, fertile soil in partial shade; ebolo is a fast-growing, soft-stemmed leafy green widely eaten across West and Central Africa and parts of Southeast Asia, where the tender young leaves and shoot tips have a distinctive bitter-savory, slightly peppery flavor often compared to a cross between spinach and arugula. It performs best with some relief from the hottest afternoon sun, which keeps leaves tender and delays the small, brush-like reddish-orange flowers that signal the plant is turning bitter and going to seed. Pinch shoot tips regularly for continuous harvest and to keep plants bushy and productive; in frost-free areas it behaves as a short-lived perennial and self-sows freely, while gardeners farther north grow it as a warm-season annual.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops & Plant Products

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions or offsets in warm, moist, rich soil in partial shade to shade once the soil is thoroughly warm; leren is strictly tropical and cannot tolerate any frost or cool soil.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in warm, consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to shade; leren is a Caribbean and northern South American relative of the ornamental Calathea houseplants, grown in dooryard gardens for the cluster of small, crisp, ivory-white tubers it forms around its base, which are boiled or steamed and eaten much like a delicate, sweet-flavored water chestnut or corn-flavored potato. The broad, upright, paddle-shaped leaves make it an attractive foliage plant for a shaded tropical bed in addition to its root crop, and clumps expand steadily by rhizome offsets that are simply divided to start new plantings or lifted for harvest. Keep soil evenly moist throughout the growing season, since dry spells check tuber development, and harvest by digging the whole clump eight to twelve months after planting once the foliage begins to decline.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops & Plant Products
CATIE (Tropical Agricultural Research and Higher Education Center)
